articles.title: Portworx Kube Datastore Reaches GA With Single-Replica Pools on FlashArray
articles.summary: Portworx manages data for VMs, containers, and AI workloads on Kubernetes across on-premises, cloud, and edge storage. Kube Datastore (KDS) groups Portworx storage pools that share a backend into a datastore, which gives VM administrators familiar datastore concepts and storage mobility on Kubernetes and gives platform engineers control over where volumes land and how much capacity they use.
bodyEvidence: Portworx by Everpure made Kube Datastore generally available today on supported SAN arrays, giving virtual machines on Kubernetes single-replica volumes backed by a shared array. Announced at KubeCon 2026, the release ships with Portworx Enterprise 3.7.2 and arrives alongside an expanded operations center, support for Red Hat OpenShift 5, and pre-staged volumes for AI inference that Everpure expects in Q1 2027.

Portworx manages data for VMs, containers, and AI workloads on Kubernetes across on-premises, cloud, and edge storage. Kube Datastore (KDS) groups Portworx storage pools that share a backend into a datastore, which gives VM administrators familiar datastore concepts and storage mobility on Kubernetes and gives platform engineers control over where volumes land and how much capacity they use.

The GA release centers on dynamic pools: a dynamic pool is a Portworx storage pool created on a shared backend, and it holds volumes with a replication factor of one, leaving data protection to the array. Portworx names Everpure FlashArray as a supported backend and has not listed other arrays. Static pools remain for workloads that need replication-based availability and for volume types that are not eligible, such as SharedV4.

The efficiency case rests on the replica count: Portworx puts the traditional shared-nothing model at roughly 2x to 3x storage overhead and 3x to 5x network I/O amplification, depending on the replication factor, and a single-replica volume on an array avoids both. When a node fails or enters maintenance, the pool moves to another node as a unit, and day 2 tasks such as rebalancing run through Kubernetes-native workflows. Portworx has not published failover times.

Portworx publishes a scale profile for Enterprise 3.7.2: up to 12 storage pools per node recommended with a hard limit of 16, up to 150 volumes and 300 snapshots per pool, up to 700 attached volumes per node, and up to 5,000 attached volumes per cluster. KDS works with KubeVirt and OpenShift Virtualization.

Portworx pairs it with array-native migration off VMware that uses FlashArray XCOPY, which the company says runs up to 12x faster than the default path, moving a 2TB VM in about two hours against more than a day. These are vendor figures, and we did not run or audit them.

“Our latest innovations, including Kube Datastore, help customers simplify storage management, recover faster from infrastructure failures, and use storage more efficiently,” said Greg Muscarella, General Manager, Portworx, at Everpure.

Pre-staged volumes target the wait before an inference service can start, when model weights that run to tens or hundreds of gigabytes are often downloaded again after a pod lands on a new node. A platform team hydrates one source volume with a versioned model bundle from an approved repository, and Portworx distributes node-local copies to eligible worker nodes and confirms each one is ready.

An inference pod is then scheduled only on a node that already holds its copy, and storage policies select the copy when a workload starts or moves. Everpure says the approach cuts storage-related startup delays and speeds recovery where AI workloads are frequently scheduled, moved, or restarted. Portworx expects pre-staged volumes in Q1 2027, says scope and timing may change, and has not published startup-time figures.

The Portworx operations center, a single in-cluster interface, now has an observability view covering pool inventory, live migration progress, and hyperconvergence state. It sits beside a topology view that maps storage nodes, pools, volumes, workloads, and VMs with health status for each object, and an alerting view that combines Portworx and Prometheus alerts with filters for severity, blast radius, and resource type.

Portworx is also opening the platform to third-party backup tools under a bring-your-own-backup (BYOB) model built on Kubernetes changed block tracking (KEP-3314), which lets a backup product copy only the blocks that changed. That support arrives with Portworx Enterprise 3.8.0, planned for early 2027, and Portworx has not named the backup products it will work with. Portworx Backup 3.2.0, planned for general availability in November, adds selective file restore for Windows VMs and IPv6-only and dual-stack networking.

Red Hat has launched OpenShift 5, and Everpure says Portworx is a launch partner, with support available at general availability in both Portworx Enterprise and Portworx CSI. Portworx already sits under OpenShift in products such as Supermicro’s edge AI appliances . Everpure also said IDC named it a Leader in the 2026 IDC MarketScape for Container Data and Infrastructure Management Software.

articles.title: CloudCasa DR Adds Dell PowerStore Failover for Kubernetes and a Read-Only MCP Server
articles.summary: PowerStore joins the HPE Alletra Storage MP B10000 , HPE Alletra 9000, and SUSE Storage as replication providers for CloudCasa DR. The division of labor is the same on each platform: the array replicates persistent volume data to the recovery site, synchronously or asynchronously in PowerStore’s case, and CloudCasa handles the Kubernetes side of failover and failback for containerized applications and KubeVirt VMs. Volume data moves array to array and never passes through CloudCasa.
bodyEvidence: CloudCasa by Catalogic has added Dell PowerStore to the storage arrays CloudCasa Disaster Recovery can drive for Kubernetes failover, alongside HPE Alletra and SUSE Storage. The same feature update adds a read-only Model Context Protocol (MCP) server that lets AI assistants check backup and DR status, and a preview of Changed Block Tracking (CBT) for KubeVirt virtual machine backups, which copies only the blocks that changed since the last run.

PowerStore joins the HPE Alletra Storage MP B10000 , HPE Alletra 9000, and SUSE Storage as replication providers for CloudCasa DR. The division of labor is the same on each platform: the array replicates persistent volume data to the recovery site, synchronously or asynchronously in PowerStore’s case, and CloudCasa handles the Kubernetes side of failover and failback for containerized applications and KubeVirt VMs. Volume data moves array to array and never passes through CloudCasa.

CloudCasa records the configuration of each protected workload in a replicated inventory volume and talks to the array through the PowerStore REST API. On failover, it brings up that inventory volume first, starts a recovery agent on the target cluster, then fails over the remaining PowerStore volume groups and rebuilds the Deployments, StatefulSets, persistent volume claims, and KubeVirt VMs against the replicated volumes. Because PowerStore fails over complete volume groups, CloudCasa advises placing workloads with different recovery requirements in separate groups.

Failback waits for operator confirmation, after which CloudCasa reverses replication on the affected volume groups so PowerStore resynchronizes only the changes made since the failover, scales down the workloads still running at the DR site, and then fails the volume groups back to the primary array and rebuilds the workloads there. CloudCasa says the approach targets recovery times measured in minutes and near-zero RPO when PowerStore replicates synchronously, with results depending on replication mode, workload size, and distance between sites.

The integration covers block (SCSI) persistent volumes provisioned through the PowerStore CSI driver; NFS and SMB volume DR is on CloudCasa’s roadmap. Supported platforms include Red Hat OpenShift and OpenShift Virtualization, SUSE Rancher/RKE2 and SUSE Virtualization, VMware vSphere Kubernetes Service, and upstream Kubernetes 1.20 and later. CloudCasa DR is licensed per worker node on an annual subscription, separately from CloudCasa’s backup product, in both the SaaS and self-hosted editions.

The MCP server lets any AI assistant that supports remote MCP servers over HTTP query CloudCasa in plain language, with questions such as which backup jobs failed in the last 24 hours or which recovery points exist for a namespace. It calls the CloudCasa APIs on the user’s behalf, authenticates with a CloudCasa API key passed in an HTTP header, and can do only what that key’s role allows. For now it is read-only: assistants can list clusters, backup policies, jobs, recovery points, restores, alerts, and backup targets, but cannot run, create, edit, or delete anything.

“Platform teams do more of their day-to-day work using AI assistants, and they want backup status available alongside the rest of their tooling,” said Ryan Kaw, Global VP of Sales and Alliances at CloudCasa. “The MCP server makes that possible today.”

The CBT preview builds on the incremental backup support KubeVirt added in version 1.8, which uses QEMU and libvirt backup capabilities and works regardless of the underlying storage. CBT records which disk blocks changed since the previous backup, so CloudCasa copies only those blocks, which the company says shortens VM backup times. On Red Hat OpenShift, that KubeVirt version arrives with OpenShift 4.22, and the feature has to be enabled explicitly.

The PowerStore DR integration and the MCP server are available now, and CBT backups remain in preview. The update also adds a dedicated VMs page that lists virtual machines across all registered clusters with their running state and guest agent status, where admins can define backups and restores for each VM.

articles.title: IBM FlashSystem Flags Data Theft in the Drive Before Ransomware Encrypts, Under 1% False Positives
articles.summary: The case IBM makes is that recovery answers the wrong question when data has already left. Recovery brings the volumes back, but it cannot tell an operator what was read out before the encryption started or how large the exposure is. IBM cites Google Cloud’s M-Trends 2026 for attackers typically spending 11 to 14 days inside a network before deploying ransomware, and its Cost of a Data Breach 2026 report for an average of 247 days to identify a breach.
bodyEvidence: IBM FlashSystem 5600, 7600, and 9600 arrays built on the fifth-generation IBM FlashCore Module now detect data exfiltration inside the drive, next to the ransomware encryption detection the modules already run. IBM says the module learns each volume’s normal read pattern, flags reads that break from it, and confirms a suspected event over a 30-minute confidence window with a validated false-positive rate below 1%. The capability is available starting in October 2026 on eligible configurations running firmware 9.1.2 or later.

The case IBM makes is that recovery answers the wrong question when data has already left. Recovery brings the volumes back, but it cannot tell an operator what was read out before the encryption started or how large the exposure is. IBM cites Google Cloud’s M-Trends 2026 for attackers typically spending 11 to 14 days inside a network before deploying ransomware, and its Cost of a Data Breach 2026 report for an average of 247 days to identify a breach.

Exfiltration is harder to catch than encryption because it is meant to look like ordinary reads. The FlashCore Module analyzes every I/O at the drive, builds a baseline for each volume, and recognizes routine backup passes and analytics scans so a scheduled full read does not trip an alert. Because the analysis runs in the module, it does not depend on endpoint agents or host logs an attacker may control, requires no application changes, and IBM says it adds no measurable performance impact.

“The future of cyber resilience is not simply recovering after an attack,” said Sam Werner, General Manager, IBM Storage. He framed the goal as identifying risk before damage occurs, with earlier insight into potential data theft and a faster response. Laurence Horrocks-Barlow, Technical Director at OCF Limited, described storage-layer detection as another stage of defense: “The sooner you know something is wrong, the sooner you can act.”

The second change targets harvest-now, decrypt-later attacks, where encrypted data stolen today is held until quantum hardware can break the key. FlashSystem keeps AES-256 for data at rest, and the fifth-generation FlashCore Module adds ML-KEM under FIPS 203 and ML-DSA under FIPS 204, two algorithms developed with IBM researchers. ML-KEM runs in hybrid mode to transport the unlock PIN to the module, and hybrid ML-DSA signatures verify firmware authenticity.

IBM says Secure HBAs will carry the post-quantum protections into the Fibre Channel data path and enable quantum-safe, session-level encryption on the fabric, without affecting efficiency, performance, or the ransomware detection running in the modules. IBM has not given a date for the HBA piece, and the session-level encryption is described as a future capability.

FlashSystem.ai, introduced with the 5600, 7600, and 9600 launch, picks up advisory capabilities in this update: contextual recommendations, task context that carries across management sessions, and suggested next-best actions. Administrators work in natural language, can see the reasoning behind a recommendation, and keep approval authority through policy-based governance. IBM puts the effort reduction for routine provisioning at up to 90%, a figure from lab-controlled evaluations of multi-volume provisioning with Safeguarded Copy and disaster recovery policies.

articles.title: Spectra Logic Storage Reclaim Packages Tape, BlackPearl, and Data Movers Into Six Configurations From 1PB to 24PB to Free Flash
articles.summary: Storage Reclaim runs in four steps. Analyze is a read-only pass over the file systems that measures how much data is inactive or infrequently accessed by age and access pattern, using what Spectra calls the Storage Analyzer. Identify applies policies, built on access, retention, and business rules, to decide which files qualify to leave flash and disk. Move and Manage moves that data to the protected tier while keeping it visible, accessible, and recallable from the original environment. Reclaim returns the freed flash and disk capacity to active workloads, AI, and future growth.
bodyEvidence: Spectra Logic today announced availability of Spectra Storage Reclaim, a packaged combination of analysis software, data movers, BlackPearl object storage, tape, and services that finds inactive unstructured data on flash and disk arrays and moves it to tape so the primary capacity can go back to active workloads. The pitch is timed to the flash market: Spectra cites contract prices up 55 to 60 percent in the first quarter of 2026 and another 70 to 75 percent in the second, with Gartner expecting a rise of almost 250 percent year over year in the second half.

Storage Reclaim runs in four steps. Analyze is a read-only pass over the file systems that measures how much data is inactive or infrequently accessed by age and access pattern, using what Spectra calls the Storage Analyzer. Identify applies policies, built on access, retention, and business rules, to decide which files qualify to leave flash and disk. Move and Manage moves that data to the protected tier while keeping it visible, accessible, and recallable from the original environment. Reclaim returns the freed flash and disk capacity to active workloads, AI, and future growth.

The data mover is a choice. Spectra’s own StorCycle handles policy-based movement, and the Storage Reclaim ecosystem also approves Komprise, Starfish Storage, and rclone, so a shop already running one of those keeps its tooling. The destination is a Spectra BlackPearl Object Gateway, which presents S3-compatible access and places data across flash, disk, and tape by policy, in front of Spectra tape storage for long-term retention with a physical air gap and no power draw for media at rest.

Spectra sells Storage Reclaim as six pre-sized configurations that bundle software, hardware, implementation, and support. The entry point is 1.05PB in a single Spectra Stack library with two half-height LTO-9 drives, and the range runs through 2.1PB and 3.0PB Stack configurations to 5.1PB, 8.1PB, and 24.3PB builds on a Spectra Cube with six to sixteen full-height drives. Spectra notes that configuration selection should be validated for the environment.

Each configuration includes a storage assessment with a written analysis report, solution planning, installation, and three years of 5×9 next-business-day support. Spectra also offers a Storage Reclaim calculator to estimate reclaimable capacity before an assessment, and its solution brief cites research putting as much as 83 percent of primary capacity in inactive data that would qualify to move, a figure Spectra attributes to a September Ctera report.

“Organizations have traditionally responded to growing storage requirements by buying more capacity. But the cheapest flash you’ll ever buy is the flash you already own,” said Nathan Thompson, CEO of Spectra Logic. “Storage Reclaim shows organizations what is consuming their existing storage capacity and moves data that no longer requires premium performance. With an ecosystem that includes Komprise, Starfish Storage, and rclone, customers can reclaim that capacity using the approach that best fits their environment.”

The product is aimed at infrastructure teams with a capacity, refresh, or budget decision in front of them, as a step before designing or buying more primary storage. That is a reasonable place to be in a year when flash allocation has become a procurement problem for AI clouds and enterprises alike, and tape media is not riding the NAND price curve. Whether a given environment has 83 percent or 20 percent of its flash holding cold files is what the read-only analysis step is there to answer.

articles.title: VAST Agent Sandbox Foundation Stack Puts NVIDIA OpenShell Sandboxes on Zero-Copy Clones and Logs Every Tool Call
articles.summary: VAST is addressing the churn that agent fleets create: thousands of isolated workspaces built and torn down in an hour, and long-running agents that sleep, resume, and hand work to short-lived sub-agents along the way. The stack decouples each agent’s persistent state from any one compute node, so an agent can pause, resume, or move to other eligible infrastructure without losing its progress or working data, and the compute can stay ephemeral while the state stays durable.
bodyEvidence: VAST Data announced the Agent Sandbox Foundation Stack with NVIDIA at NVIDIA GTC Berlin, a reference architecture that runs NVIDIA NemoClaw agents inside NVIDIA OpenShell sandboxes on the VAST AI Operating System. OpenShell handles isolated execution and policy enforcement around each agent, and VAST handles the parts that have to outlive the sandbox: the agent’s workspace, its memory and context, and a record of every action it took. VAST says the design is meant to run thousands of agents and sub-agents in production without tying their state to whichever compute node happens to be running them.

VAST is addressing the churn that agent fleets create: thousands of isolated workspaces built and torn down in an hour, and long-running agents that sleep, resume, and hand work to short-lived sub-agents along the way. The stack decouples each agent’s persistent state from any one compute node, so an agent can pause, resume, or move to other eligible infrastructure without losing its progress or working data, and the compute can stay ephemeral while the state stays durable.

When a new agent task starts, the VAST DataStore Block CSI driver provisions a persistent volume for the OpenShell sandbox from a zero-copy clone, which VAST says takes seconds and avoids a full copy of the underlying data. In the reference implementation VAST published on GitHub under an Apache 2.0 license, each workflow gets a head persistent volume claim, and each sub-agent gets a clone of it; volume snapshots cover suspend and resume, and a sleeping sandbox keeps its volume.

VAST DataBase serves as the shared vector store and knowledge base, which VAST says lets hundreds of reasoning agents query the same dataset concurrently without a copy per agent. In the GitHub implementation, it also holds per-department agent memory, the trace spans and turns, and the finished reports, and a Model Context Protocol server is the only path from a sandbox to the database. NemoClaw supplies the agent layer and supports Hermes, LangChain, OpenClaw, or a custom harness.

“Every enterprise that puts an agent into production will eventually need to answer what it did and why it did it,” said Alon Horev, CTO and Co-Founder at VAST Data. “An agent might exist for minutes, spawn thousands of other agents and then disappear, but its work has to persist and its actions have to stay understandable long afterward.”

OpenShell applies identity-based access and behavior policies and logs every interaction between an agent and anything outside its sandbox. VAST DataBase keeps the durable copy of that record, logging every tool call, prompt, token, cost, and decision so the audit trail survives after the agent and its sandbox are gone. The VAST Management System adds real-time telemetry on data flows across the fleet, and VAST says that telemetry interoperates with NVIDIA Sentry , the BlueField-4 DPU layer that monitors traffic between agents on Vera CPUs and models on Rubin GPUs.

When Sentry flags or quarantines a misbehaving agent, VAST says the AI OS isolates that agent’s data access and freezes the sandbox state for forensic review. “As AI agents take on more complex work, enterprises need infrastructure that can support secure execution while preserving the data, context and state agents depend on across their lifecycle,” said Kari Briski, Vice President of Generative AI Software at NVIDIA.

Foundation Stacks are VAST’s packaging of NVIDIA AI Blueprints into repeatable deployments on the AI OS. The first two covered an enterprise research assistant on VAST DataEngine with NVIDIA Nemotron and video intelligence on NVIDIA Cosmos reasoning models with NVIDIA Video Search and Summarization; this one covers the agent runtime itself. It also builds on VAST DataEnclave , the confidential computing runtime VAST previewed in September, and on the OpenShell reference architecture NVIDIA detailed at the same show.

VAST is demonstrating the stack at GTC Berlin with a governed multi-agent workflow in which agents spawn, pull from persistent data services, and keep their state as the compute underneath them changes. The GitHub implementation runs that pattern as a supervised research job: a lead agent plans the work on an NVIDIA NIM model, a human can approve or edit the plan, and sub-agents run in parallel inside OpenShell sandboxes against an earnings-call corpus in VAST DataBase.

VAST has not published a general availability date, required software versions, or hardware configurations for the stack, and the thousands-of-agents figure is a design target with no measured provisioning rate or concurrency result behind it.

articles.title: NVIDIA JUPITER Quantum Simulation Models a 104-Qubit Fault-Tolerant Processor Across 8,192 GH200 GPUs and 512 TiB
articles.summary: Earlier Jülich work simulated 50 qubits under ideal, noiseless conditions, and this run keeps the noise in. The 104 physical qubits cover the data and auxiliary qubits across the whole protocol, which starts a magic state in a distance-3 color code, adds flag measurements to catch harmful faults, grows it into a distance-7 hybrid color and surface code, and finishes with further error-correction rounds and readout. The noise model goes beyond random bit and phase flips to coherent phase errors that can accumulate and interfere, and selected sites carry a third energy level so the simulation captures leakage out of the computational states.
bodyEvidence: NVIDIA has run a 104-qubit simulation of a fault-tolerant quantum processor on JUPITER , Europe’s first exascale supercomputer at the Jülich Supercomputing Centre, using 8,192 GH200 GPUs. Announced ahead of GTC Berlin, the run models magic state cultivation, a method of producing the non-Clifford states a fault-tolerant computer consumes during logical operations, under realistic hardware noise. NVIDIA calls it the largest comprehensive simulation of a fault-tolerant quantum processor to date and says cultivation needs 90 percent fewer qubits than previous methods, a comparison the company does not spell out.

Earlier Jülich work simulated 50 qubits under ideal, noiseless conditions, and this run keeps the noise in. The 104 physical qubits cover the data and auxiliary qubits across the whole protocol, which starts a magic state in a distance-3 color code, adds flag measurements to catch harmful faults, grows it into a distance-7 hybrid color and surface code, and finishes with further error-correction rounds and readout. The noise model goes beyond random bit and phase flips to coherent phase errors that can accumulate and interfere, and selected sites carry a third energy level so the simulation captures leakage out of the computational states.

The state is a full state vector, with no Clifford shortcuts for the non-Clifford operations that prepare the magic state. The encoded register comes to 45 bits, about 35.2 trillion complex amplitudes, which occupy 512 TiB of distributed GPU memory in double precision, or 64 GiB on each of the 8,192 GPUs, with room left for communication and analysis.

NVIDIA’s simulator reorders operations while preserving dependencies and measurement statistics, reuses storage as qubits are measured and released, and packs the three-level sites into binary storage, so five of them (243 basis states) fit in eight bits. In small cases, independent tensor-network calculations matched the state-vector results to about one part in 10 trillion.

A GB200 NVL72 system at the NVIDIA Accelerated Quantum Research Center served as the development platform. Researchers scaled tests from four GPUs to hundreds there, compared results against JUPITER, and studied how accuracy changed with more compute before committing the full 8,192-GPU allocation, which NVIDIA says cut a week-long simulation effort to days. The run uses cuQuantum’s cuStateVec library for the state-vector evolution, with cuBLASMp and cuSOLVERMp factoring selected partitions of the stored state so approximate methods can be checked against the full reference. The cultivation circuit is expressed through the fault-tolerant logical layer of CUDA-Q .

Kristel Michielsen, director of the Jülich Supercomputing Centre at the Forschungszentrum Jülich facility, said: “Europe’s investment in JUPITER gives researchers the ability to investigate questions that were previously beyond reach.” NVIDIA’s stated goal for the work is to connect the error propagation it observed to the quality and cost of logical operations, so hardware teams can weigh designs before fabricating them. No logical error rates, fidelities, or runtimes have been published for the run so far.

articles.title: HPE Spaceborne Computer-4 Will Run AI Inference on the Moon Aboard Astrolab’s FLIP Rover
articles.summary: HPE’s Dr. Mark Fernandez, principal investigator for HPE Spaceborne Computer-2, holds a mockup of HPE Spaceborne Computer-4. The entire system is contained in an approximately 249 mm by 132 mm by 26 mm aluminum chassis.
bodyEvidence: HPE announced HPE Spaceborne Computer-4, a compute module that will run AI inference and what HPE says will be the first HPC benchmarks on the Moon. Loaded with KIOXIA SSDs, the module will fly as a payload on Astrolab’s FLIP rover, which Voyager Technologies’ Griffin-1 lander will deliver near the lunar south pole. Launching in late 2026, this mission is part of NASA’s Commercial Lunar Payload Services (CLPS) initiative, which aims to bring scientific, exploration, and technology payloads to the Moon from commercial vendors.

HPE’s Dr. Mark Fernandez, principal investigator for HPE Spaceborne Computer-2, holds a mockup of HPE Spaceborne Computer-4. The entire system is contained in an approximately 249 mm by 132 mm by 26 mm aluminum chassis.

HPE invited us to a press event at Astrolab’s Hawthorne, California facility. The event included a one-hour panel featuring Francisco Cordova, COO of the ISS National Laboratory; HPE’s Scott Wiest; Astrolab’s CEO Jaret Matthews; and KIOXIA’s Faraz Velani. The panel discussion was followed by a tour of the facility, including what will become mission control (powered by HP Omen systems) and its IT infrastructure, which runs on HPE Alletra Storage and HPE Private Cloud PC3000.

We were also given a tour of the clean room and an up-close look at the actual Moon-bound FLIP rover. We learned about the rover, its mission, and how HPE’s Spaceborne Computer-4 will help process scientific data from FLIP’s instruments on-prem (which is such a weird way to describe the surface of the Moon ).
Francisco Cordova, Faraz Velani, Scott Wiest, and Jaret Matthews sit on a panel moderated by HPE’s Norm Follett next to a mockup of FLIP.

Astrolab’s FLIP rover sits in their clean room ready for launch at the end of 2026. The vertical flat piece is the back of the solar panel, which will deploy in this position, since FLIP will work at the lunar south pole where the Sun is always on the horizon during the lunar day.

Let’s start with FLIP, the Flex Lunar Innovation Platform. It’s a Lunar rover developed by Astrolab. It features several scientific payloads and, of course, HPE Spaceborne Computer-4. The rover will land on the Moon’s south pole to provide research and data for a potential Moon base. The south pole is of particular interest because the craters there are in perpetual darkness and may contain large amounts of water ice, a valuable resource for a future Moon base.

FLIP’s most obvious feature is its large wheels, designed by Venturi, which will allow it to traverse the difficult Lunar regolith. I couldn’t confirm whether they were inspired by Cadillac’s classic wire wheels, but I have my suspicions. FLIP is intended to evaluate and mature several components and subsystems for FLEX, Astrolab’s future rover, including full-sized batteries, tires, avionics systems, sensors, and software.

The software evaluations are where HPE Spaceborne Computer-4 comes in, aiming to do as much AI inference and processing on-prem (the “prem” here is the Moon’s south pole) as possible. The software stack runs in a container on a Linux-based operating system.

For benchmarking, HPE will run High-Performance LINPACK (HPL) to evaluate the sustained performance Spaceborne Computer-4 can provide in a constrained environment, and High-Performance Conjugate Gradient (HPCG) to evaluate performance characteristics under workloads that stress memory access and communication patterns. These benchmarks will help characterize how the system will run workloads in a lunar environment, providing invaluable technical data for future missions. It’s also just cool to submit a benchmark with the location set to “the Moon.”

There will also be a few core AI applications, including an LLM RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) to show how an LLM can integrate mission-specific information for more context-aware insights at the lunar edge (The Lunar Edge is a great band name). This can also be used on Earth to search text-dense mission documents more efficiently.

HPE isn’t the only one with workloads on the module. NASA will run its Federated Learning for Unbounded and Intelligent Decentralization (FLUID) experiment, an AI neural net trained on data from Earth, the Moon, and the International Space Station, to demonstrate coordination of three separate AI models, along with a tuned LLM test for searching and interpreting onboard documents. Deloitte’s Silent Shield, a new intrusion detection system, will provide near real-time predictive cyber-analytics and anomaly detection.
Pictured are some of FLIP’s instruments, including a headlight, camera array, LiDAR, and image projector. Also included is an American Flag patch that went to the Moon during the Apollo program.

HPE Spaceborne Computer-4 will also evaluate LLM vision inference. This workload is intended to analyze and interpret the data from the rover’s many cameras. Performing visual inference locally can enable the system to identify or interpret information without continuously transmitting the underlying visual data to Earth. This is especially useful given FLIP’s location at the Moon’s south pole, where data rates back to Earth are quite slow.

LiDAR data will also be processed for mapping, navigation, and terrain analysis. Particularly for navigation, LiDAR processing is necessary for the rover to navigate safely on the lunar surface. Because a round trip to the Moon takes at least 2.6 seconds at the speed of light, and longer once ground processing is added, real-time control of FLIP is impossible and, like the Mars rovers, FLIP must navigate on its own.
KIOXIA’s Faraz Velani stands next to HPE’s Dr. Mark Fernandez, who is holding a mockup of Spaceborne Computer-4. There are two 1TB KIOXIA BG6 SSDs in the module. (Photo courtesy of HPE).
On the hardware side, the Spaceborne Computer-4 is a purpose-built compute module adapted to the unique constraints of a lunar rover, like power, heat, and form factor.

For power, the rover runs at 28 VDC and has limited wattage to spare. Spaceborne Computer-4 has a low-power CPU and GPU from an undisclosed company, and storage from KIOXIA, a long-time partner for the Spaceborne systems. The storage is an off-the-shelf BG6 from KIOXIA’s client storage line, but it has a power-limiting feature enabled that caps usage at 5W. Apparently, it’s been available on most KIOXIA drives for many years, but no one on Earth (not hyperbole) wants to limit drive performance. It was, however, perfect for this use case.

For heat management, the Spaceborne Computer-4 is in a bespoke aluminum chassis and is integrated into the rover’s thermal management system. In fact, some of the heat the system produces can be used to help keep the rest of the rover warm, particularly during the lunar night, when surface temperatures fall to around -280 F and lower still in the shadowed polar craters. The system is fanless because there’s no air on the Moon, obviously. The chassis and its components have been optimized for the rover’s form factor and weigh only 2.6 pounds.

Astrolab CEO Jaret Matthews shows where FLIP will be deployed on the Moon’s south pole. The blue-shaded areas are crater basins that are in perpetual darkness and may contain large amounts of water ice.

Another major consideration for lunar operations is exposure to cosmic rays. Here on Earth, our atmosphere absorbs most cosmic rays and charged particles from the Sun. Bit-flips, or Single-Event Upsets (SEUs), happen, but are very rare here on Earth. On the Moon, FLIP is pretty much in open space, with no magnetic field or atmosphere to protect the onboard electronics. I asked about hardware shielding and space hardening, and the answer is there’s surprisingly very little on the Spaceborne Computer-4, if any. In discussions with HPE, they told me about space hardening with software. There are two KIOXIA drives that are mirrored, but beyond that, the resiliency comes from the software checking and double-checking itself. You trade some CPU cycles for this, but it is ultimately worth it to ensure reliability.
HPE’s Spaceborne Computer-2 onboard the International Space Station (Photo by NASA).

HPE Spaceborne Computer-4 is just the latest system HPE has designed specifically for space use; Spaceborne Computer-2 has been doing scientific work aboard the International Space Station for years. Bill Hewlett and David Packard even have a history with the Apollo program, and some of HP’s earliest products and instruments were used on the US’s first satellites in the late 1950s. This deployment will be exciting to watch, and I look forward to all the scientific insights FLIP and Spaceborne Computer-4 will provide. See you in the stars!

articles.title: Smarter, Safer, More Sustainable: How Valeo is Engineering the Future of Global Trucking Fleets
articles.summary: Valeo’s innovations are designed to help fleet operators address their most pressing challenges by providing the hardware and software necessary to optimize the total cost of ownership.
bodyEvidence: September 1, 2026 — Paris, France — Valeo, a global leader in automotive and commercial vehicle technologies, is participating in IAA Transportation 2026 , the world’s leading platform for logistics, commercial vehicles, the transport sector and solutions for the mobility of tomorrow. From September 14 to 20 , Valeo will showcase its latest solutions for heavy-duty trucks and light commercial vehicles at the Hanover Messe (Hall 20 booth 30).
Valeo’s innovations are designed to help fleet operators address their most pressing challenges by providing the hardware and software necessary to optimize the total cost of ownership.

Detlef Juerss, Valeo Chief Sales and Business Development Officer said: “The IAA Transportation is a key platform for the global commercial vehicle industry – an important market and focus area for Valeo. Our commercial vehicle OE customers value our innovative products and solutions as they enhance safety, reduce cost, provide comfort and create a differentiating design for their customers. We are proud to have gained the trust of our OE customers with a significant increase of orders since the last IAA in all the segments we serve. Specifically for the electrified, autonomous and software-driven truck, we see a growing demand for our technologies – core businesses for Valeo. Particularly our ADAS sensor, sensor cleaning and compute technology are supporting all levels of autonomy – a game changer for the industry.”
15 September: The future of Autonomous Transport / Main Stage

As the commercial vehicle industry undergoes a major transformation fueled by new safety and environmental regulations, as well as by the transition to autonomous trucking , Valeo is positioning itself as the key partner for commercial truck manufacturers navigating this complexity. With electric trucks projected to take a substantial global market share by 2030 and autonomous trucking expected to grow rapidly in the next decade, Valeo is ready to support this evolution.

Valeo continues to build on its strong presence in historical products, such as lighting, wipers, powertrain systems and thermal management, while drastically accelerating its leadership in high-growth technologies including electrification, advanced driver assistance systems (ADAS) up to Level 4 autonomy , and software-defined vehicle technologies (SDV).
Committed to global regulatory standards, Valeo enhances in-cabin safety while improving the driving environment and making vehicle behavior predictable for everyone, both on and off the road.

Valeo’s Adaptive Driving Beam (ADB) technology automatically shapes high-beam headlights around oncoming traffic, maximizing nighttime visibility for drivers without blinding other road users. Long established as a standard for passenger cars, Valeo is now introducing this crucial glare-free lighting solution to the commercial vehicle market.

Inside the cabin, Valeo provides a safe interior environment by pairing cutting-edge hardware with sophisticated software solutions. A key feature of this high-performance cockpit is the advanced Driver Monitoring System (DMS) , which actively tracks driver drowsiness and distraction to ensure full compliance with stringent GSR II and NCAP 2026 standards.

Remanufacturing is key for Valeo in the aftermarket, and integrated into the “I Care 4 the Planet” program initiated by the Group to progressively reduce the environmental impact of the automotive sector. Valeo is significantly broadening its aftermarket reman range, which now features more than 6,000 references across four primary categories: starters and alternators, brake calipers, air conditioning compressors, and transmission parts—including clutches and pneumatic concentric actuators for commercial vehicles.
Recently, Valeo accelerated its REMAN 2.0 program, expanding into electronic (eg. NOx sensors) and electrification parts (eg. Inverters, EDCs).
Valeo aims to reuse more than 80% of materials on average and drastically reduce CO 2 emissions, delivering ‘as good as new’ quality at an attractive cost.

About Valeo Valeo is a leading global technology company creating innovative solutions and systems for automotive and technology partners worldwide. Valeo is structured around its POWER, BRAIN and LIGHT Divisions, and Valeo Service, the augmented service partner, for the aftermarket and new forms of mobility. Valeo is committed to making mobility safer, more sustainable and affordable to all. The Group is playing a vital role in shaping the Car of Tomorrow: which will be electrified, safer and software-defined. Valeo is leveraging its global industrial footprint and its technological leadership in electrification, advanced driver assistance systems, lighting and software to capture an increasing share of value per vehicle. Valeo is listed on the Paris Stock Exchange. Valeo in brief: €20.9 billion in sales in 2025 | 100,000 employees worldwide | 29 countries | 149 production plants | 59 R&D centers | 19 distribution platforms (as of February 26, 2026). articles.title: Valeo Accelerates Future Lighting at its Angers Plant
articles.summary: The integration of new optical technologies is supported by an active recruitment and training policy.
bodyEvidence: The Angers site finalizes its modernization plan to produce complex, new-generation lighting systems.
The integration of new optical technologies is supported by an active recruitment and training policy.
The factory establishes itself as a European reference for the fast-growing heavy goods vehicle segment.

July 2, 2026 — Paris, France — The Valeo industrial site in Angers, a historic French hub of expertise in the design and production of automotive lighting systems, is finalizing the rollout of its modernization plan.

Automotive lighting is a high-growth market in which Valeo is a global leader. Conducted between 2023 and 2026 and representing an investment of more than 45 million euros, the plan has transformed the workshops and deployed new optical technologies to meet the growth targets outlined in the Valeo Elevate 2028 strategic plan. Accompanied by recruitment momentum, this transformation illustrates the local roots and global technological reach of the Anjou plant.

Jean-Luc Terrasse, CEO of Valeo’s Light Division , said: “ Lighting is at the heart of the mobility challenges of tomorrow: safety, design, and intelligent interaction with the environment. It allows manufacturers to differentiate themselves and offer users ever-increasing safety and driving comfort. This 45 million euro investment allows the factory to consolidate its industrial excellence. The Angers site demonstrates that a French factory can design and produce systems of unprecedented optical complexity and be at the forefront of European Industry 4.0.”

The Angers plant showcases the Group’s expertise and its high standards for quality, operational performance, and industrial competitiveness. It is firmly rooted in its region, focusing on industrial innovation and operational excellence.

With over 1,200 highly qualified employees across Angers and Blois, Valeo’s industrial operations in the region supply 9,000 headlights and 22,000 complex modules daily to the world’s leading manufacturers. The site benefits from exceptional innovation capabilities through its dual DNA, which combines industrial excellence with advanced R&D design.

Valeo has been selected by several European manufacturers to equip their new vehicles with complex bi-color optical lenses. The modernization plan has enabled a major transformation of the thermoplastic injection workshops, equipping them with new, dedicated, high-performance automated injection press lines.
The plant now features a high-tech industrial facility equipped with 25 injection presses, 5 varnishing lines, 11 assembly lines, and 181 robots.

The site also benefits from significant innovation strength through its R&D center, with 24 projects currently under development, including 6 major projects specifically allocated to the Angers plant.
All these processes benefit from the increasing integration of digital tools and Artificial Intelligence for predictive simulation and real-time system validation.
To support these industrial advancements, the teams remain Valeo’s priority:

The market for utility and heavy duty vehicle lighting is currently very dynamic. With two major launches planned in 2027 and 2028 for new clients, the site’s production volume related to heavy goods vehicles will increase from 20% to 40% . By 2030, 6 out of 7 European road transport leaders will be driving with headlights developed in Angers.
The Angers site has been designated the Product & Process Competence Center for Heavy Duty Vehicle front headlights at the European level for the entire Group.
